Assets are the hard part of making a realistic FPS this way, more than code. Claude Code is good at gameplay code (movement, weapons, AI, netcode) and can drive the game editor through MCP plugins. It can't make realistic models, animations or sound, and it can't play your game, so playtesting falls to you. You'll also need to run Claude Code on your Mac itself; the engine and editor have to be local.

## Engine options (all run on Apple Silicon)

| | Realism ceiling | Mac support | How well Claude Code fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unreal Engine 5** | Highest (Lumen, Nanite, free Megascans) | Works, but Mac gets less support: slow C++ builds through Xcode, and some plugins are Windows-only | C++ is fine. Blueprints are binary files, so Claude can only change them through MCP |
| **Unity 6 (HDRP)** | High | Good | Very good: C# plus an official MCP |
| **Godot 4** | Medium; hard to make look realistic | Excellent | Best: scenes and scripts are all text |

## Ways to connect Claude Code to the engine

- **Unity (official):** Unity's own MCP requires Unity 6 (6000.0) or later with the com.unity.ai.assistant package installed. It ships a Mac Apple Silicon relay binary, and you must approve the connection before the client can invoke tools. The main community alternative is Coplay MCP (community) — for Unity 2022+.
- **Unreal (all community-made, none official):**
  - runreal's server leverages the built-in Python remote execution capabilities, so it needs no custom plugin.
  - UEMCP is another no-compile option; it installs with `claude mcp add unreal -- uvx uemcp`.
  - aadeshrao123's UnrealMCP is broader: it uses a C++ plugin and covers 280 commands: materials, blueprints, niagara, statetree, actors.
  - Quality varies, so expect some rough edges.
- **Godot:** There are several free servers, for example GDAI MCP, Coding-Solo, bradypp, satelliteoflove.

## Getting realistic assets (Claude can't make these)

- **Starting projects:** Unreal's First Person template, or Lyra (Epic's full shooter sample project). On Unity, the Starter Assets FPS controller. Starting from one of these saves weeks.
- **Environments:** Quixel Megascans and Fab (free or cheap with Unreal), or the Unity Asset Store.
- **Characters and animation:** Mixamo is fine for prototyping. Realistic weapon handling usually needs a paid FPS animation pack.
- **AI 3D generation** (Meshy, Tripo): fine for props, but I wouldn't expect it to produce hero assets that look realistic yet. That's my judgment, not something I benchmarked.

## Recommendation

- **Realism matters most:** Unreal 5 with Lyra or the FPS template, an Unreal MCP server, and Claude writing the gameplay in C++. Expect friction on Mac. I'm not certain how fully Nanite and Lumen match the Windows versions on Apple Silicon right now, so check Epic's release notes for your UE version before committing.
- **Smoothest Claude Code workflow:** Unity 6 HDRP with the official Unity MCP. It's a little less realistic but much less friction on Mac.
- **Either way:** put a `CLAUDE.md` in the project with the engine version and your conventions, and have Claude read the editor console or logs after each change. Without that it's coding blind.

What kind of "unusual" you mean decides the whole stack. There are three cases, and in the hardest one the earlier recommendation reverses: Unreal stops being a good choice.

## Three kinds of "weird space"

| Kind | Examples | Is space flat up close? | Normal engines OK? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Portals / weird topology** | Impossible rooms, wraparound worlds (a 3-torus, where leaving one side brings you back the other), Manifold Garden-style repetition | Yes | Yes. Standard physics and netcode work; you add portal rendering and ghost copies at seams. |
| **B. Walking on a sphere's surface** | Tiny planets, Mario Galaxy | Yes | Yes. It's just custom gravity. |
| **C. Truly curved 3D space** | The 3-sphere S³, hyperbolic space H³, the other Thurston geometries | No | No. The renderer, physics, culling, lighting and netcode all assume ordinary flat space. |

"Spherical topological space" sounds like C (S³). If it's really A or B, my earlier answer mostly still stands.

## What case C involves

- **Positions:** You store everything as 4×4 matrices acting on 4D coordinates instead of normal 3D transforms. For S³ these are 4D rotations; for H³ they're Lorentz-type transforms. The projection to the screen happens in a vertex shader.
  - The common Unity approach does the entire computation in the vertex shader, which lets you keep the original vertex buffers, use the standard matrices, animation scripts.
- **S³ quirks:** Light wraps all the way around, so every object appears twice (near and antipodal) and you can see the back of your own head. You need two-hemisphere rendering or the "elliptic" variant of S³, plus care with the depth buffer. For gameplay, this means bullets can come at you from "behind" after going around the world.
- **Lighting:** Shadows, global illumination, screen-space effects and frustum culling are all built for flat space, so they'll be wrong or need rewriting. Truly curved space and a realistic look pull against each other. Hyperbolica-style flat shading is realistic to aim for; Lumen-quality lighting isn't.
- **Physics:** You write it yourself. An FPS needs fairly little: a character controller, hitscan along geodesics (straight lines in curved space, which are great circles in S³ and closed-form and cheap) and simple collision shapes using geodesic distance. That's doable.
- **Multiplayer:** You replicate those matrices (or pairs of unit quaternions for S³), not Vector3s. You'd drop built-in pieces like NetworkTransform and write custom state syncing. For S³, interpolating between snapshots uses slerp, which suits it well. Re-normalize the matrices every so often to stop numerical drift. Lag compensation rewinds the same group elements.

## Engines, revised for case C

- **Unreal:** Drop it. Nanite, Lumen, shadows and culling would all work against you.
- **Unity (URP plus custom shaders):** This route has the most precedent. CodeParade tackled the problem in Unity without relying on portals in Hyperbolica and released the Non-Euclidean Unity Backend for Hyperbolica (HyperEngine) as reference code. You also get the official MCP and C#.
- **Godot 4:** The engine is open source, so you can change the renderer, and every file is text, which suits Claude Code best. It has built-in multiplayer, and it's excellent on Mac.
- **Custom (Rust with wgpu/Bevy, or TypeScript with WebGPU/three.js):** Since you'll replace transforms, rendering and physics anyway, an engine mostly buys you input, audio, asset loading and an editor. A browser build also makes multiplayer playtesting trivial (send a link), and Claude can screenshot it with Playwright. For exotic geometries, the reference is ray-marching: algorithms that produce accurate real-time interactive in-space views of the eight Thurston geometries using ray-marching.

For case C I'd lean Godot or a custom web/Rust stack, then Unity. That's a judgment call, not a benchmarked result.

## Getting the most out of Claude Code here

- **Separate geometry library first:** Build the math (isometries, geodesics, distance, parallel transport, which keeps your orientation consistent as you move) as its own module, and have Claude write property tests for it. For example: isometries preserve distance, and walking a geodesic for its full length 2π in S³ returns you to the start. Claude is strongest on verifiable math like this, and it can't see visual bugs on its own.
- **Order of work:** single-player S³ renderer and hitscan, then server-authoritative networking, then art.
- **Art:** Low-poly or stylized assets distort more gracefully under curved projection than photoreal ones.

Sources:
- [HyperEngine (Hyperbolica's Unity backend)](https://github.com/HackerPoet/HyperEngine)
- [CodeParade's Non-Euclidean Engine](https://digitalproduction.com/2020/07/06/die-etwas-andere-game-engine/)

content.text:
# Pages

An artifact is a web page this server hosts at a claude.ai link. These are the rules the server applies.

## What a page is

- One complete HTML document. Begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>: content that does not read as HTML is refused. To publish a Markdown document, write an HTML page from its content.
- A page published as one document carries its own CSS, JavaScript, data and images (data: URIs or inline SVG); only the libraries and fonts listed below load from outside. A page published from files may also load its own files by relative path.
- Give it a <title>. On a new artifact pass the same words as title.
- Put viewport-fit=cover in its viewport meta only with env(safe-area-inset-*) padding: the Claude iOS app draws such a page under its top bar.
- A page can be up to 16 MiB.

## What a page may load

The page runs under a content security policy. Apart from the artifact's own files, anything not listed here is blocked by the browser, with no error on the page.

- Scripts: inline, or from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/python-visualization/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com, code.jquery.com, cdn.plot.ly.
- Stylesheets: inline, or from fonts.googleapis.com. A library's stylesheet from any other host must be inlined or shipped as one of the page's own files.
- Fonts: from fonts.gstatic.com (through a Google Fonts stylesheet), or inlined as data: URIs.
- Images and media: data: and blob: URIs. A remote image does not load.
- fetch, XMLHttpRequest and WebSocket to other hosts are blocked.

## What the viewer's frame allows

The page runs in a sandboxed frame.

- Refused or ignored: alert, confirm and prompt; window.print; downloads the page starts, by <a download> or by script; clipboard reads (the viewer's own paste works); camera, microphone, location, motion, screen capture and Web Share; service workers; WebRTC; <object>, <embed> and iframes of other sites. Build dialogs into the page, offer a Copy button where you would offer an export, and offer no button for the others unless a capability (last item) provides it.
- Link to other sites with a plain <a href>, which the viewer opens outside the page; window.open fails for most viewers.
- mailto:, tel: and other non-web links fail for many viewers: keep the link, show the address or number as text too, and never report a message as sent.
- A form has nowhere to submit: handle submit in script, with preventDefault().
- Call these only from a click handler, and catch a refusal: navigator.clipboard.writeText, fullscreen, pointer lock, audio playback.
- These work: file inputs and dropped files (use them in place of the camera and microphone), Web Workers from the page's own files or blob: URLs.
- localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB keep data in one viewer's browser. It survives a republish, reaches no other viewer or device and not Claude, and may be missing or throw: use try/catch and render well without it. Use it only for one viewer's conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, an unsent draft), never for state that must last.
- Only a plain #name passes between the artifact's URL and location.hash, never #/path, #key=value, a pushState path or a query string. The address bar on the artifact's own page and Share's Copy link follow the page's hash; beside a chat, in a project or in an app the bar may not. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending, route on the hash: name each in ASCII letters, digits and hyphens such as #costs-emea (never settings, sidebar, customize, upgrade, downloads or comment-*, which claude.ai reserves) and show the one in location.hash, or the start view if none, on load and on hashchange.                        lambda r: r.fulfill(status=200, content_type="application/javascript", body=THREE))
        await pg.goto((ROOT / "index.html").as_uri())

        async def shot(name, js=None, wait=600):

I've built and published both new demos: a hyperbolic block world and a block world with black holes you can place. I loaded each one in headless Chrome and checked the screenshots; there were no console errors.

**Hyperbolic demo (H³)**
- **"Parallel" walls:** seven straight walls all leave one base wall at right angles, 3 blocks apart. In flat space they'd stay parallel; here they fan apart exponentially. The "Above the rails" button shows this best.
- **Ground tiles:** the stone roads outline identical squares whose corners are 72°, so five meet at every crossing instead of four.
- **Flying up:** the ground is an infinite plane, but from high up it shrinks to a small ball-like disk below you.
- **Readout:** shows the circumference of a circle around where you started, next to what it would be in flat space.

**Black hole demo**
- **How it's drawn:** every pixel is a light ray traced backwards along its real general-relativity path, so it's actual lensing, not a screen-space filter.
- **What emerges from that:**
  - a black shadow about 2.6× the horizon size;
  - an Einstein ring with a mirrored image of the whole scene;
  - blocks near a hole look redder and dimmer;
  - the outside world looks bluer if you fly close.
- **Optional accretion disk:** gives the familiar Interstellar look, brighter on the side moving toward you.
- **Thrown balls** stretch out toward the hole, slow down, redden and fade at the horizon, which is what a distant observer would really see.

**Where I traded realism for playability**
- **Several holes:** light bending is exact for one hole; with several, I add their effects together, which is an approximation.
- **Ball gravity:** I weakened it. A real hole this size would weigh about 50 Earths, and everything nearby would fall in instantly.
- **Ball stretching:** exaggerated so you can see it.

**Performance:** the black-hole demo is heavy on the graphics chip, so it renders at reduced resolution by default. The quality menu lets you raise it. I couldn't measure frame rate, because the test browser draws in software.

**Sharing it, including with other agents**
- **People:** each demo is private to you until you share it from its page on claude.ai. I can't change sharing from here.
- **Other agents (the better route):** put the three HTML files in a git repo with a short notes file covering the math each demo relies on:
  - the 4D-coordinates trick for both curved spaces;
  - how moving and turning are done as 4D rotations;
  - the light-bending equation and how it's stepped through the voxel grid.

  A Claude Code agent opening that repo reads the notes first, so the physics is respected without re-explaining it each time. I can write the notes and push the repo to GitHub if you want; the `gh` command line tool is available here.
- **Making the physics reusable:** the math sits in a few small, self-contained parts of each file. Pulling those into one JavaScript module (and later a Rust or C# port for a real engine) is the step that makes it reusable for the multiplayer game.

The source for all three demos is attached as `index.html` (the 3-sphere), `hyperbolic.html` and `blackholes.html`.

**Hyperbolic demo (H³)**
- **"Parallel" walls:** seven straight walls all leave one base wall at right angles, 3 blocks apart. In flat space they'd stay parallel; here they fan apart exponentially. The "Above the rails" button shows this best.
- **Ground tiles:** the stone roads outline identical squares whose corners are 72°, so five meet at every crossing instead of four.
- **Flying up:** the ground is an infinite plane, but from high up it shrinks to a small ball-like disk below you.
- **Readout:** shows the circumference of a circle around where you started, next to what it would be in flat space.

**Black hole demo**
- **How it's drawn:** every pixel is a light ray traced backwards along its real general-relativity path, so it's actual lensing, not a screen-space filter.

chat_messages.text:
**Short answer:** it depends on how latency-sensitive the stateful logic is. Most real systems run two separate paths:

1. **Fast-paced games (shooters, fighting, physics):** connect the client directly to an authoritative game server. Don't put a relay hop in between.
2. **Everything else (lobby, chat, presence, matchmaking, turn-based or slow-tick games, collaborative apps):** use a gateway tier of thin connection servers in front of sharded stateful backends. This is close to what you described.

**Pattern 1: direct to a dedicated game server**
- A matchmaker or allocator (e.g. Agones, GameLift, or your own) picks a server process for the match. It returns `ip:port` plus a short-lived auth token, and the client connects straight to that server.
- One process (or thread) owns a match or room in memory and runs a fixed tick (20–128 Hz). It handles client inputs and sends back state snapshots or deltas.
- Use UDP for this traffic (ENet, a custom reliable-UDP layer, or QUIC). From a browser, use WebTransport or WebRTC data channels. TCP and WebSocket suffer head-of-line blocking: one lost packet holds up every packet behind it, which hurts at 60 Hz. WebSocket is fine for slower games; many .io games ship on it.
- Why no gateway here: an extra hop adds serialization, queuing and jitter, and it buys you little. A match only lasts minutes, so it doesn't matter that a deploy can't keep the connection alive.

**Pattern 2: gateway tier plus stateful shards**
- **Gateways** keep the client sockets and do TLS, auth, heartbeats, rate limiting and fan-out. They hold only connection state, no business state. You scale them on connection count and memory.
- **Stateful backends** are sharded by entity (room, channel, guild, user). Route with consistent hashing or a directory service so each entity has exactly one owner, often modeled as an actor.
- **Gateway to backend:** a small number of long-lived, multiplexed streams, such as gRPC bidirectional streams or a custom framed TCP protocol. Don't open one backend connection per client.
- **Cross-shard broadcast:** use pub/sub (NATS, Redis, Kafka). It's fine for chat, but too slow and costly for per-tick game state.
- **What it buys you:** you can deploy game logic without dropping client sockets, the backends don't need to be publicly reachable, and connection scaling is separate from compute scaling. Slack and Discord both use roughly this shape.
- **What it costs:** one more hop, plus the job of rerouting when shards move.

**Efficiency details that matter more than topology**
- Batch outgoing traffic per tick instead of sending on every event. Coalesce writes so you make fewer syscalls.
- Use binary encodings (protobuf, FlatBuffers, or bit-packed custom formats), delta compression, and interest management (only send what's near the player).
- Give each connection a bounded send queue for backpressure. Drop or disconnect slow consumers rather than buffering without limit.
- Use event-loop I/O (epoll or io_uring, or runtimes built on it such as Go, Tokio, Netty or the BEAM). Per-connection buffers usually dominate memory, so size them carefully.
- Use L4 load balancers for long-lived connections. Raise file-descriptor limits, and watch ephemeral port use on the gateway-to-backend links.
- Support session-resume tokens so a client can reconnect after a network blip. On deploys, drain connections gradually so you don't trigger a reconnect stampede.

**What I'd do:** for an action game, use a gateway path for the meta systems and direct UDP to an allocated game server for matches. For an MMO-ish or slow-tick game, or any non-game real-time app, use the gateway plus consistent-hashed stateful shards. Either way, keep the gateways thin; if you put game logic in them, a deploy drops every player's connection. Some MMOs do proxy all game traffic through a gateway (zone servers behind front-end proxies), but they accept the extra latency because players move between zone servers.

What you're after is realistic in 2026, with one limitation you should know about: you can write nearly everything in Rust, but Rust's memory-safety guarantees mostly stop at the edge of the GPU kernel.

**The limitation**
Rust's ownership model doesn't describe thousands of SIMT threads sharing global and shared memory. Inside a kernel, the main bug classes (cross-thread data races, missing barriers, out-of-bounds indexing when you compute it yourself) are still yours to prevent. Even NVIDIA's own project concedes this: its docs say GPU memory safety remains a work in progress, so some unsafe blocks may still be required. The real safety gains are on the host side: typed buffers, lifetimes tied to command submission, and safe launch wrappers. That's where most of the code, and most real-world bugs, actually live.

**What to use where**

| Need | Pure-Rust option | Maturity |
|---|---|---|
| Graphics, cross-platform | **wgpu**: runs natively on Metal, Vulkan and DX12 | Production. Shaders are WGSL by default, but wgpu supports shaders in WGSL, SPIR-V, and GLSL and converts them for any backend |
| Shaders written in Rust | rust-gpu → SPIR-V → wgpu/naga → MSL on Mac | Works in principle. I haven't verified how robust it is on Metal, so test early |
| Portable compute (Apple, NVIDIA, AMD) | **CubeCL**: a single #[cube] Rust function compiles on demand to CUDA, HIP, Metal, SPIR-V, WGSL, or CPU SIMD | Most mature of these; Burn runs on it in production |
| NVIDIA-specific kernels | **cuda-oxide** (NVIDIA Labs): single-source Rust compiled to PTX. Alternatively Rust-CUDA, which has been rebooted | Alpha. It's Early alpha as of September 2026 and requires a specific nightly Rust toolchain from April 2026 |
| AMD-specific | CubeCL's HIP backend; otherwise HIP C++ over FFI | No dedicated Rust-to-AMDGPU path that I know of |
| Apple CPU | NEON intrinsics are stable; SME/AMX need asm or Accelerate (as in my last answer) | NEON is solid; SME/AMX are rough |

**Suggested architecture**
1. **Safe Rust core** for application logic, scheduling and memory management. No `unsafe` here.
2. **A small hardware-abstraction crate**: a backend trait whose implementations are your only `unsafe` code. Keep it small and audited.
3. **CubeCL as the default kernel language**, so you get one Rust-syntax source for every vendor.
4. **Native-language kernels only where profiling demands it**: MSL on Apple, CUDA C++/PTX or CUTLASS on NVIDIA. Load them behind the same safe trait. Expect very few.
5. **Differential testing**: check every kernel against a plain-Rust CPU reference, with randomized shapes. This replaces the guarantees the borrow checker can't give you inside kernels.

**Peak-performance caveat**
On recent NVIDIA hardware (Hopper wgmma/TMA, Blackwell tcgen05), the state of the art in GEMM and attention lives in CUTLASS, cuDNN and Triton. Rust DSLs generally trail on the newest tensor-core features, and I haven't confirmed how close CubeCL gets on those parts. Before committing a hot path, benchmark CubeCL against cuBLAS (or MPS on Apple) for your actual shapes.

For a Mac-first FPS where you want Rust and a custom engine, there are three realistic stacks, plus non-Rust engines for comparison.

**1. Rust + wgpu, your own engine (my default recommendation)**
- Rust all the way through. The engine runs natively on Metal, and you can add Vulkan/DX12 later for almost nothing.
- Recent wgpu releases close many of the old gaps. v28 added mesh shaders, which are fully supported on Vulkan, and supported on Metal and DX12 with passthrough shaders, plus multiview on Metal.
- Costs: some CPU overhead from wgpu's validation and resource tracking (measure it with your draw counts; it may not matter). It also doesn't expose Apple-specific features: memoryless attachments, tile shaders, Metal 4, MetalFX.
- Workaround: wgpu's `as_hal` gives you the underlying Metal objects, so you can call MetalFX or other native features through objc2 for specific passes.

**2. Rust + objc2-metal directly, with a thin rendering abstraction you write yourself**
- The best possible performance and features on Mac: MetalFX upscaling and frame interpolation, argument buffers and bindless, explicit control of the tile memory Apple GPUs render through.
- The cost is that you build a whole rendering layer, and every port later means another backend (for example `ash` for Vulkan). Only worth it if profiling of stack 1 shows wgpu is the bottleneck, or you need Metal 4 features throughout.

**3. Bevy, with a customized or replaced renderer**
- The fastest route to something playable in Rust: ECS, assets, windowing and input all solved, running on wgpu.
- Costs: breaking API changes every few months, and you're adapting someone else's architecture rather than building your own. A reasonable hybrid is using just `bevy_ecs` and a few other Bevy crates inside your own engine.

**For comparison, non-Rust options**
- **Godot**: a native Metal driver for Apple Silicon, which owes a lot to the work of the MoltenVK project. Rust works via the godot-rust (gdext) bindings. Good if you'd rather not write an engine.
- **Unreal 5**: the strongest FPS feature set, but it's C++, and as I understand it Mac has historically been a second-tier platform for it.

**Libraries for a Rust FPS**
